modules.name: Jan Vansina
modules.outcome: Decide whether a spoken tradition can be used as a source, and mark what it can and cannot tell you.
modules.intro: Vansina (1929 to 2017) was a Belgian historian of Central Africa who made oral tradition a respectable historical source. His method asks what the tradition is, who carried it, and what pressures shaped it.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia gives his dates and says he was a major innovator in the historical methodology of oral tradition, and that David Beach judged his 1985 Oral Tradition as History to have made nearly all earlier frameworks obsolete. {{wiki-vansina}} The Oral tradition page reports his working definition and the 1960s debate he started. {{wiki-oral}}
Confidence in this dossier: partial. His own books were not read, so the method below is the encyclopaedic summary plus the working library's account of his advice. {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Check the definition. A message counts as oral tradition if it is spoken, sung or played on an instrument and passed on by word of mouth over at least a generation. {{wiki-oral}}
Treat reverence for speech as a fact about the society. Vansina compares the attitude of an oral society to speech with a literate society's reverence for the written word. {{wiki-oral}}
Look for compressed genealogies and the floating gap between the founding past and recent memory. {{lib}}
Ask who tells it and why now, because tellers shape accounts for present politics. {{lib}}
Collect by fieldwork where you can. Historians who gathered traditions in person broke from the habit of working only in archives and libraries. {{wiki-oral}}

modules.name: Ibn Khaldun
modules.outcome: Test a ruler's story against how groups and dynasties actually work, before you accept it.
modules.intro: Ibn Khaldun (1332 to 1406) lived between the Maghrib and Cairo and wrote a famous introduction to history. Here we borrow one idea of his, group solidarity, to question a ruler's account.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says his Muqaddimah introduced the idea of asabiya (group feeling or solidarity), stresses the human capacity to think and to cooperate in a division of labour, and that his historical method had few precedents or followers in his own time. {{wiki-khaldun}}
Confidence: partial. We did not read the Muqaddimah. Our application to Ethiopian sources below is our own inference, not his words.
His method, step by step

i: Ask what holds the group together. For Ibn Khaldun the key word is asabiya. {{wiki-khaldun}}
Ask how people cooperate. He argues that no individual can supply all his needs and that people cooperate to do so. {{wiki-khaldun}}
Ask whether the story fits that picture. A dynasty that claims divine descent but shows no organised group behind it should raise questions (our application).
Ask who wrote it. His own career as a judge and adviser to rulers suggests that writers of history can serve patrons (our inference). {{wiki-khaldun}}

modules.name: Ibn Khaldun
modules.outcome: Read a Maghribi dynasty story alongside what you know about how groups rise and fall, and mark where evidence ends.
modules.intro: Ibn Khaldun's life was spent among Maghribi dynasties. In 1384 the Egyptian sultan made him professor at the Qamhiyyah madrasa and chief Maliki judge in Cairo, where he found his reform efforts resisted. His group-feeling idea gives a lens for the Almoravids and Almohads.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia reports the 1384 appointment, that he resigned the judgeship within a year, that a ship carrying his family sank off Alexandria in 1384, and that he took part in the campaign against Timur at Damascus in 1400 to 1401. {{wiki-khaldun}}
Confidence: partial. We did not read the Muqaddimah. Applications to the Almoravids and Almohads are our inference.
His method, step by step

i: Name the group. The Almoravids were a Sanhaja Berber movement led by Abd Allah ibn Yasin and Yusuf ibn Tashfin. {{lib}}
Name what united it. The library describes a preacher and commanders; asabiya is our lens, not a claim of the library. {{wiki-khaldun}}
Name the successor. The Almohads were led by Ibn Tumart and Abd al-Mu'min, who took Marrakesh in 1147. {{lib}}
Ask what happened next. For the Ghana story, remember that the traditional account of an Almoravid conquest rests on thin and late sources. {{lib}}
Keep the historian's career in view. His own record as an official shows how political posts shaped writing. {{wiki-khaldun}}

modules.name: Ibn Battuta
modules.outcome: Weigh a travel account as an eyewitness with known weaknesses, using Mali in 1352 to 53 as the test case.
modules.intro: Ibn Battuta (born 24/02/1304, Tangier) travelled from 1325 and dictated his Rihla in 1354 to 55. His Mali chapters are the best eyewitness account we have, with real strengths and real chronological problems.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia gives his birth date and the start of his pilgrimage on 14/06/1325, his visit to the Mali capital and its ruler Mansa Suleyman, king since 1341, the fact that he mistook the Niger for the Nile, and that he dictated the account to Ibn Juzayy after the Marinid ruler asked for it. {{wiki-battuta}}
Confidence: partial. We did not read the Rihla. The library calls the Mali account the best eyewitness account. {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Note when and for whom it was recorded. He dictated it to Ibn Juzayy after returning in 1354. {{wiki-battuta}}
Note what he saw. He praised Mali's justice and safety and criticised some customs. {{lib}}
Note his errors. He took the Niger for the Nile, so geography is not safe. {{wiki-battuta}}
Note the chronology problem. Scholars find that some of his dated stages cannot all be right. {{wiki-battuta}}
Compare with other sources. Check al-Umari and the Sundiata epic on the same state. {{lib}}

head: Strength

blocks.title: Use and caution
steps: Use him for what a visitor saw: the court, safety on the roads, the ruler's name.
Do not use him for Musa's 1324 to 25 pilgrimage, which he did not see.
Do not trust his dates where scholars find the chronology confused. {{lib}} {{wiki-battuta}}

modules.name: Samuel Johnson
modules.outcome: Read an African-authored history with its aims, informants and editing in view.
modules.intro: Samuel Johnson (1846 to 1901) was a Yoruba clergyman born in Sierra Leone who finished The History of the Yorubas in 1897. It is one of the main African-authored sources for Oyo and its neighbours.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. A Boston University biography says he was born in Hastings, Sierra Leone, ordained in the 1880s, pastor at Oyo from 1887, finished the history by 1897, and wrote from patriotic motives; his brother Obadiah rewrote the book from his papers and it appeared in 1921. {{bu-johnson}} Cambridge University Press describes it as bringing together oral and recorded accounts, and repeats the story of the lost manuscript. {{cup-johnson}}
Confidence: partial. We did not read the book beyond the front-matter excerpt. The library calls it an African-authored history that mixes tradition and documentary work. {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Start with the author's stated aim. Johnson says he wrote from patriotic motives, so that the history would not be lost. {{bu-johnson}}
Note his informants. The preface thanks the Timi of Ede, Lagunju, as a gifted and trusty historian. {{ia-johnson}}
Note his position. He was an Anglican pastor at Oyo who saw Christianity as crowning, not overturning, Yoruba history. {{bu-johnson}}
Note the editing. The manuscript was lost and reconstructed by his brother, so the 1921 text is partly Obadiah's work. {{cup-johnson}}
Cross-check with other evidence such as Robin Law's study of Oyo. {{lib}}

modules.name: Ibn Battuta
modules.outcome: Use a traveller's description of a Swahili town while holding its date and aims in view.
modules.intro: Ibn Battuta reached the East African coast during his early travels, and his remarks on Kilwa are among the few eyewitness lines on the Swahili towns.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says he arrived at Kilwa, then a transit centre of the gold trade, described it as one of the finest and most beautifully built towns, and recorded a visit in 1330 while the library gives 1331. It notes that his stated chronology for the early 1330s has problems. {{wiki-battuta}}
Confidence: partial. We did not read the Rihla. We do not know which date is right.
His method, step by step

i: Note the claim. He found Kilwa among the most beautifully built towns. {{wiki-battuta}}
Note the date range. His visit is c. 1330 to 1331, and the library uses 1331. {{wiki-battuta}} {{lib}}
Note what archaeology adds. The library points to coral-rag stone buildings, the palace of Husuni Kubwa and a great mosque. {{lib}}

Note a mismatch. The quoted passage says the buildings were of wood with reed roofs, while the library points to coral-rag stone buildings, so compare them with excavation (our observation). {{wiki-battuta}} {{lib}}
Write the date as about 1330 to 1331.

modules.name: Jan Vansina
modules.outcome: Apply the oral-tradition method to Zulu testimony and say what the recording date does to it.
modules.intro: Vansina's rules for oral sources apply to the James Stuart Archive and to the Shaka stories alike.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. The Oral tradition page reports the working definition and the debate in which Vansina and his students developed a rigorous approach to recovering the past from oral traditions. {{wiki-oral}} It also reports a later view that discrepancies between traditions can signal problems, shifts and struggles, and that the presentist critique, that traditions are shaped by the present, is hard to dismiss. {{wiki-oral}}
Confidence: partial. The Stuart archive was not read; the library describes it. {{lib}}
His method, step by step

i: Identify the type. The James Stuart Archive records testimony from Zulu elders in the early 20th century. {{lib}}
Count the gap. Shaka died in 1828, so testimony recorded around 1900 to 1920 is about 70 to 90 years later (our arithmetic).
Compare versions. Differences between versions are signals, not noise. {{wiki-oral}}
Ask who benefits now. Present politics shape what is remembered. {{wiki-oral}}
Place trader accounts beside testimony and note the interests of each. {{lib}}

blocks.title: Zulu sources compared (our grid built on the library)
head: Source
Recorded
Interest

blocks.x: Worked example: counting the gap (our arithmetic)

blocks.title: How long after?
steps: If a testimony is recorded in 1905 about Shaka, who died in 1828, the gap is 1905 minus 1828, which is 77 years.
A speaker aged 70 in 1905 was born in 1835, seven years after Shaka's death, so cannot have seen him.
So the speaker relies on what others told them. Tag the account as tradition. {{lib}}

blocks.w: That is the later emphasis reported on the Oral tradition page. {{wiki-oral}}

blocks.w: 1905 minus 70 is 1835. This is our arithmetic.

i: Count the gap between event and recording. {{wiki-oral}}

modules.name: Olaudah Equiano
modules.outcome: Use a first-person narrative of the Atlantic trade while keeping the records that complicate it beside it.
modules.intro: Olaudah Equiano (c. 1745 to 1797) published The Interesting Narrative in 1789. It is one of the earliest widely read writings by an African in England, and its account of his origins is disputed.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read encyclopaedic pages in excerpt form on 30/10/2026, not his own work. Wikipedia says the Narrative went through nine editions in his lifetime, was a best seller by 1792, and shaped the antislavery movement. It also reports that Vincent Carretta found a 1759 baptism record listing him as born in Carolina and a naval muster pointing to South Carolina, that Carretta called the circumstantial evidence compelling but not absolutely conclusive, and that other scholars think the weight of evidence supports Equiano's own account. {{wiki-equiano}}
Confidence: partial. We did not read the Narrative.
His method, step by step

i: Note the genre. It is the first influential slave narrative, but his experience was unusual: he did not do field work and learned to read and write. {{wiki-equiano}}
Note the aim. It was published to support antislavery campaigning in Britain. {{wiki-equiano}}
Put the records beside the text: baptism 1759, muster roll, the Narrative itself. {{wiki-equiano}}
Tag the birthplace claim as contested.
Use the narrative for what is not disputed: the experience of the trade and its audience.

blocks.x: Worked example: reading age against date (our arithmetic)

blocks.title: Check the age

The commonly given c. 1745 differs by about two years. State a range.
Whatever the birthplace, use the Narrative with the Voyages data in Module 8 for scale. {{wiki-equiano}} {{sv-est}}
